chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 1
paragraphs: "Well, Prince, so Genoa and Lucca are now nothing more than estates belonging to the Bonaparte family. But I'm warning you — if you don't tell me this means war, if you keep on defending the atrocities committed by that Antichrist — and I truly believe he is the Antichrist — then I'm done with you. You are no longer my friend, no longer my 'faithful slave,' as you like to call yourself! But how are you? I can see I've frightened you — sit down and tell me all the news." (in French)

It was July 1805, and the speaker was the well-known Anna Pavlovna Scherer, lady-in-waiting and favorite of the Empress Marya Fedorovna. These were the words with which she greeted Prince Vasili Kuragin, a man of high rank and influence, who was the first to arrive at her reception. Anna Pavlovna had been coughing for several days. She was suffering from la grippe, as she put it — grippe being a fashionable new word in St. Petersburg at the time, used only by the elite.
All of her invitations, without exception written in French, had been delivered that morning by a footman in scarlet livery. They all read the same way:

"If you have nothing better to do, Count (or Prince), and if the prospect of spending an evening with a poor invalid isn't too terrible, I would be delighted to see you tonight between seven and ten. — Annette Scherer." (in French)

"Good heavens! What a fierce attack!" replied the prince, not at all put out by this reception. He had just walked in wearing an embroidered court uniform with knee breeches and buckled shoes, decorations glinting on his chest, his flat face wearing a look of calm self-assurance. He spoke in that refined French in which an earlier generation not only conversed but thought, and with the gentle, patronizing tone that comes naturally to a man of importance who has grown old in the ways of society and the court. He walked up to Anna Pavlovna, kissed her hand, offered her a view of his bald, perfumed, gleaming head, and settled himself comfortably on the sofa.

"First of all, dear friend, tell me how you are. Put your friend's mind at rest," he said (in French), his tone unchanged — beneath the politeness and the show of sympathy, one could detect indifference, even irony.

"How can anyone be well when they're suffering morally? How can anyone stay calm in times like these, if they have any feeling at all?" said Anna Pavlovna. "You are staying the whole evening, I hope?"
"And the party at the English ambassador's? Today is Wednesday. I need to put in an appearance there," said the prince. "My daughter is coming to pick me up."
"I thought today's event had been canceled. I must say, all these celebrations and fireworks are becoming tiresome."
"If they had known you wished it, the entertainment would have been postponed," said the prince, who, like a wound-up clock, said things out of habit that he didn't even expect to be believed.
"Don't tease! Well, and what has been decided about Novosiltsev's dispatch? You know everything."

"What can one say about it?" replied the prince in a cold, indifferent tone. "What has been decided? They've decided that Bonaparte has burned his bridges, and I believe we are prepared to burn ours."

Prince Vasili always spoke in a languid drawl, like an actor going through a stale role. Anna Pavlovna, on the other hand, despite her forty years, overflowed with energy and passion. Being an enthusiast had become her social calling, and sometimes, even when she didn't feel like it, she would work herself into a state of enthusiasm so as not to disappoint the people who expected it of her. The faint smile that always played around her lips — though it didn't really suit her faded features — expressed, like a spoiled child's, a constant awareness of her charming weakness, which she neither wished, nor could, nor saw any reason to correct.
In the middle of a conversation about politics, Anna Pavlovna burst out:

"Oh, don't speak to me about Austria! Perhaps I don't understand these things, but Austria has never wanted war and doesn't want it now. She is betraying us! Russia alone must save Europe. Our gracious sovereign understands his sacred duty and will remain true to it. That is the one thing I believe in! Our good and noble sovereign must fulfill the highest role on earth, and he is so virtuous and noble that God will not abandon him. He will fulfill his calling and crush the monster of revolution, which has become more terrible than ever in the person of this murderer and villain! We alone must avenge the blood of the righteous. Who else can we count on? England, with her commercial mentality, will never understand Emperor Alexander's nobility of soul. She has refused to leave Malta. She looks for hidden motives behind everything we do. What answer did Novosiltsev get? None. The English have not understood, and cannot understand, the selflessness of our Emperor, who seeks nothing for himself but only the good of humanity. And what have they promised? Nothing! And the little they have promised, they won't deliver! Prussia has always insisted that Bonaparte is invincible and that all of Europe is powerless against him. And I don't believe a word Hardenberg says, or Haugwitz either. This famous Prussian neutrality is nothing but a trap. I have faith only in God and in the noble destiny of our beloved sovereign. He will save Europe!"
She broke off suddenly, smiling at her own intensity.

"I think," said the prince with a smile, "that if you had been sent instead of our dear Wintzingerode, you would have taken the King of Prussia's consent by storm. You are so eloquent. Will you give me a cup of tea?"

"In a moment. By the way," she added (in French), growing calm again, "I'm expecting two very interesting men tonight: the Vicomte de Mortemart, who is connected to the Montmorencys through the Rohans — one of the finest French families. He is one of the true émigrés, the genuine ones. And also the Abbé Morio. Do you know that brilliant thinker? He has been received by the Emperor. Had you heard?"

"I shall be delighted to meet them," said the prince. "But tell me," he added with studied casualness, as though the thought had only just occurred to him — though the question he was about to ask was the real reason for his visit — "is it true that the Dowager Empress wants Baron Funke appointed as first secretary at Vienna? From what I hear, the baron is a rather mediocre fellow."
Prince Vasili wanted this post for his own son, but others were trying, through the Dowager Empress Marya Fedorovna, to secure it for the baron.
Anna Pavlovna half-closed her eyes, as if to indicate that neither she nor anyone else had any right to question what the Empress desired or approved of.
"Baron Funke has been recommended to the Dowager Empress by her sister," was all she said, in a dry, sorrowful tone.

As she mentioned the Empress, Anna Pavlovna's face suddenly took on an expression of deep and genuine devotion and respect, mixed with sadness — and this happened every time she spoke of her illustrious patroness. She added that Her Majesty had been gracious enough to show Baron Funke a great deal of esteem, and her face clouded over with sadness once more.

The prince said nothing and looked unconcerned. But with the womanly quickness and social instinct that came naturally to her, Anna Pavlovna wanted both to reproach him — for daring to speak that way about someone recommended by the Empress — and at the same time to console him, so she said:
"Now about your family. Do you know that since your daughter came out in society, everyone has been captivated by her? They say she is astonishingly beautiful."
The prince bowed to express his respect and gratitude.

"I often think," she continued after a short pause, moving closer to the prince and smiling warmly, as if to signal that politics and social topics were finished and it was time for personal conversation — "I often think how unfairly the joys of life are sometimes distributed. Why has fate given you two such wonderful children? I'm not talking about Anatole, your youngest. I don't like him," she added in a tone that left no room for argument, raising her eyebrows. "Two such charming children. And yet you appreciate them less than anyone, which means you don't deserve them."
And she flashed her rapturous smile.
"I can't help it," said the prince. "Lavater would have said I lack the bump of fatherly feeling."

"Don't joke. I mean to have a serious talk with you. Do you know I'm unhappy with your younger son? Between ourselves" — and her face took on its melancholy expression — "he was mentioned at Her Majesty's court, and you were pitied..."
The prince said nothing, but she looked at him meaningfully, waiting for a reply. He frowned.

"What would you have me do?" he said at last. "You know I did everything a father could for their education, and they've both turned out to be fools. Hippolyte is at least a quiet fool, but Anatole is an active one. That's the only difference between them." He said this with a smile more natural and animated than usual, so that the lines around his mouth clearly revealed something unexpectedly coarse and unpleasant.
"And why are children born to men like you? If you weren't a father, there would be nothing I could reproach you with," said Anna Pavlovna, looking up thoughtfully.
"I am your faithful slave, and to you alone can I confess that my children are the curse of my existence. It is the cross I have to bear. That's how I explain it to myself. What can be done?"
He said no more, but conveyed his resignation to a cruel fate with a gesture. Anna Pavlovna reflected for a moment.

"Have you ever thought of marrying off your wayward son Anatole?" she asked. "They say old maids have a passion for matchmaking, and though I don't feel that weakness in myself just yet, I do know a young woman who is very unhappy with her father. She's a relation of yours — Princess Mary Bolkonskaya."
Prince Vasili did not reply, but with the quick memory and social perception of a man of the world, he gave a slight nod of the head to show he was considering the idea.

"Do you know," he said at last, clearly unable to hold back the gloomy current of his thoughts, "that Anatole is costing me forty thousand rubles a year? And," he went on after a pause, "what will it be in five years if he carries on like this?" After a moment he added, "That's what we fathers have to deal with. Is this princess of yours wealthy?"

"Her father is very rich and very miserly. He lives in the country. He's the famous Prince Bolkonski who had to retire from the army under the last Emperor and was nicknamed 'the King of Prussia.' He's very clever but eccentric, and a bore. The poor girl is very unhappy. She has a brother — I think you know him — he recently married Lise Meinen. He's an aide-de-camp to Kutuzov and will be here tonight."

"Listen, dear Annette," said the prince, suddenly taking Anna Pavlovna's hand and for some reason pulling it downward. "Arrange that match for me and I shall be your most devoted slave forever — 'slave' with an f, as one of my village elders writes in his reports. She is rich and from a good family, and that's all I need."

And with the easy, familiar grace that was so natural to him, he raised the lady-in-waiting's hand to his lips, kissed it, and swung it gently back and forth as he leaned back in his armchair, looking off in another direction.

"Wait," said Anna Pavlovna (in French), thinking it over. "I'll speak to Lise — young Bolkonski's wife — this very evening, and perhaps the thing can be arranged. It will be on your family's behalf that I begin my apprenticeship as an old maid."

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 2
paragraphs: Anna Pavlovna's drawing room was gradually filling up. The highest society of Petersburg was gathered there: people who differed widely in age and temperament but who all belonged to the same social world. Prince Vasili's daughter, the beautiful Helene, came to collect her father for the ambassador's party; she wore a ball gown and her badge as lady-in-waiting. The youthful little Princess Bolkonskaya, known as the most captivating woman in Petersburg (in French), was also there. She had married the previous winter and, being pregnant, no longer attended large gatherings — only small receptions. Prince Vasili's son Hippolyte had arrived with Mortemart, whom he introduced. The Abbé Morio and many others had come as well.
* La femme la plus séduisante de Pétersbourg.

To each new guest Anna Pavlovna said, "You haven't yet seen my aunt," or "You don't know my aunt?" — and with great solemnity she escorted each one over to a little old lady wearing large ribbon bows in her cap, who had come sailing in from another room as soon as the guests began arriving. Slowly turning her eyes from the visitor to her aunt, Anna Pavlovna would announce each person's name and then leave them.

Every guest went through the ritual of greeting this old aunt whom none of them knew, none of them wanted to know, and none of them cared about. Anna Pavlovna watched these greetings with mournful, solemn interest and silent approval. The aunt said the same thing to each of them: she asked about their health and spoke of her own, and about the health of Her Majesty, who "thank God, was feeling better today." And each guest, though politeness prevented them from showing impatience, left the old woman with a sense of relief at having performed an annoying obligation, and did not go near her again for the rest of the evening.

The young Princess Bolkonskaya had brought some needlework in a gold-embroidered velvet bag. Her pretty little upper lip, on which a faint dark down was just visible, was too short for her teeth, but this only made it curl up more sweetly, and was especially charming when she sometimes drew it down to meet her lower lip. As is always the case with a truly attractive woman, her flaw — the shortness of her upper lip and her half-open mouth — seemed to be her own unique and special form of beauty. Everyone brightened at the sight of this pretty young woman, so soon to be a mother, so full of life and health, carrying her burden so lightly. Old men and bored, dispirited young ones who spent time in her company and talked with her felt as though they too were becoming, like her, full of life and energy. Everyone who spoke with her, watching at each word her bright smile and the constant gleam of her white teeth, thought themselves to be in an especially good mood that day.

The little princess circled the table with quick, short, swaying steps, her workbag on her arm, and cheerfully spreading out her skirts, sat down on a sofa near the silver samovar as though everything she did was a pleasure to herself and to everyone around her. "I've brought my work," she said (in French), showing her bag and addressing the whole room. "Mind you, Annette, I hope you haven't played a trick on me," she added, turning to her hostess. "You wrote that it would be just a small gathering — and look how badly I'm dressed." And she spread her arms wide to show off her short-waisted, lace-trimmed, elegant gray dress, cinched with a broad ribbon just below the bust.
"Don't worry, Lise — you will always be prettier than anyone else," replied Anna Pavlovna (in French).

"You know," said the princess in the same tone of voice, still in French, turning to a general, "my husband is abandoning me? He's going off to get himself killed. Tell me — what is this awful war even for?" she added, turning to Prince Vasili, and without waiting for an answer she turned to speak to his daughter, the beautiful Helene.
"What a delightful woman this little princess is!" said Prince Vasili to Anna Pavlovna.

One of the next guests to arrive was a heavyset young man with close-cropped hair, spectacles, and the light-colored trousers that were fashionable at the time. He wore a very high collar ruffle and a brown dress coat. This stout young man was the illegitimate son of Count Bezukhov, a well-known grandee from Catherine the Great's era, who was now lying on his deathbed in Moscow. The young man had not yet entered either the military or the civil service, having only just returned from abroad where he had been educated; this was his first appearance in society. Anna Pavlovna greeted him with the minimal nod she reserved for the lowest tier of her drawing room hierarchy. But despite this cold welcome, a look of anxiety and alarm crossed her face when she saw Pierre enter — as though something too large and unsuited to the room had appeared. And although he was certainly bigger than the other men present, her unease could only have stemmed from the clever yet shy, observant yet natural expression that set him apart from everyone else in that drawing room.
"It is so good of you, Monsieur Pierre, to come visit a poor invalid," said Anna Pavlovna (in French), exchanging an anxious look with her aunt as she led him over.
Pierre mumbled something inaudible and kept looking around as though searching for something. On his way to the aunt, he smiled warmly at the little princess, as one does to a close acquaintance.

Anna Pavlovna's alarm proved justified, for Pierre turned away from the aunt without waiting to hear her remarks about Her Majesty's health. Anna Pavlovna caught him in dismay and said, "Do you know the Abbé Morio? He is a most interesting man."
"Yes, I've heard about his plan for perpetual peace, and it's very interesting — but hardly practical."

"You think so?" said Anna Pavlovna, wanting to say something before escaping to attend to her duties as hostess. But Pierre now committed a second social blunder. First he had walked away from a lady before she finished speaking to him; now he continued talking to someone who clearly wanted to get away. With his head bent forward and his big feet planted wide apart, he launched into an explanation of why he considered the abbé's plan unrealistic.
"We'll discuss it later," said Anna Pavlovna with a smile.

Having rid herself of this young man who didn't know how to behave, she went back to her duties as hostess, continuing to observe and listen, ready to step in wherever the conversation might stall. Like the foreman in a spinning mill who, after setting the workers to their tasks, walks around noticing where a spindle has stopped or where one is creaking or making too much noise, and hurries to slow it down or get it running properly — so Anna Pavlovna moved through her drawing room, approaching first a group that had gone quiet, then one that had grown too loud, and with a word here or a slight adjustment there, she kept the conversational machine running smoothly and steadily. But through all of this, her anxiety about Pierre was obvious. She watched nervously whenever he drifted near the group around Mortemart to listen in, and again when he moved on to the circle gathered around the abbé.

Pierre had been educated abroad, and this evening at Anna Pavlovna's was the first society reception he had attended in Russia. He knew that all the intellectual stars of Petersburg were gathered here, and like a child in a toy shop, he didn't know which way to look, afraid of missing some brilliant conversation. Seeing the self-assured, polished expressions on the faces around him, he kept expecting to hear something truly profound. At last he made his way over to Morio. The conversation there seemed interesting, and he stood waiting for a chance to share his own views, the way young people always do.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 3
paragraphs: Anna Pavlovna's reception was in full swing. The spindles hummed steadily and ceaselessly on all sides. Aside from the aunt — beside whom sat only one elderly lady whose thin, careworn face seemed rather out of place in this brilliant company — the entire gathering had arranged itself into three groups. One, mostly male, had formed around the abbé. Another, made up of younger people, clustered around the beautiful Princess Helene, Prince Vasili's daughter, and the little Princess Bolkonskaya, who was very pretty and rosy-cheeked, though perhaps a bit plump for her age. The third group was gathered around Mortemart and Anna Pavlovna.

The vicomte was a good-looking young man with soft features and polished manners, who clearly considered himself a celebrity but was modest enough, out of politeness, to make himself available to whatever circle he found himself in. Anna Pavlovna was clearly serving him up as a treat for her guests. Just as a skilled chef presents as a rare delicacy a cut of meat that no one who had seen it in the kitchen would have wanted to eat, Anna Pavlovna offered up first the vicomte and then the abbé as especially choice morsels. The group around Mortemart immediately began discussing the murder of the Duc d'Enghien. The vicomte said that the duc had perished because of his own noble nature, and that Bonaparte had particular reasons for hating him.
"Ah, yes! Do tell us all about it, Vicomte," said Anna Pavlovna (in French), pleased that the phrase had a certain Louis XV ring to it: "Contez nous çela, Vicomte" — tell us the story, Vicomte.
The vicomte bowed and smiled graciously to show his willingness to oblige. Anna Pavlovna arranged a group around him, inviting everyone to listen to his story.

"The vicomte knew the duc personally," Anna Pavlovna whispered to one guest. "The vicomte is a marvelous storyteller," she told another. "You can tell at once he belongs to the very best society," she said to a third. And so the vicomte was served up to the company in the finest possible style, like a beautifully garnished roast on a silver platter.
The vicomte was about to begin his story and gave a subtle smile.
"Come here, Helene dear," said Anna Pavlovna to the beautiful young princess who was sitting some distance away, at the center of another group.

The princess smiled. She rose with the same unchanging smile she had worn since entering the room — the smile of a flawlessly beautiful woman. With a light rustle of her white dress trimmed with moss and ivy, with a gleam of white shoulders, glossy hair, and sparkling diamonds, she passed between the men who stepped aside for her. She looked at none of them, yet smiled at all of them, as though graciously granting each one the privilege of admiring her beautiful figure and shapely shoulders, back, and bosom — which, as was the fashion, were very much on display — and she seemed to bring the glamour of a ballroom with her as she crossed toward Anna Pavlovna. Helene was so stunning that she showed not the slightest trace of flirtation; on the contrary, she almost seemed embarrassed by her own overwhelming beauty. She appeared to wish, but to be unable, to lessen its effect.

"How lovely!" said everyone who saw her; and the vicomte lifted his shoulders and lowered his eyes as if startled by something extraordinary when she took her seat across from him and turned her unchanging smile upon him as well.
"Madame, I doubt my abilities before such an audience," he said (in French), smiling and inclining his head.

The princess rested her bare, rounded arm on a small table and evidently felt no reply was needed. She waited with a smile. Throughout the story she sat upright, glancing now at her beautiful round arm, its shape slightly altered where it pressed against the table, now at her still more beautiful bosom, where she adjusted a diamond necklace. From time to time she smoothed the folds of her dress, and whenever the story produced a particular effect, she glanced at Anna Pavlovna, instantly adopted the same expression she saw on the hostess's face, and then settled back into her radiant smile.
The little princess had also left the tea table and followed Helene.
"Wait a moment — let me get my work. Now then, what are you thinking about?" she said, turning to Prince Hippolyte. "Fetch me my workbag."
There was a general stir as the princess, smiling and chatting merrily with everyone at once, sat down and cheerfully arranged herself in her seat.
"Now I'm all settled," she said, and asking the vicomte to begin, she picked up her needlework.
Prince Hippolyte brought over the workbag, then joined the circle and pulled a chair up close to hers, seating himself beside her.

The charming Hippolyte was remarkable for his extraordinary resemblance to his beautiful sister, but even more remarkable for the fact that, despite this resemblance, he was strikingly ugly. His features were like his sister's, but while in her case everything was illuminated by a joyous, self-satisfied, youthful, ever-present smile and by the wonderful classical beauty of her figure, his face was dulled by a look of imbecility and an expression of sullen self-importance, while his body was thin and weak. His eyes, nose, and mouth all seemed scrunched into a vacant, weary grimace, and his arms and legs always settled into unnatural positions.
"This isn't going to be a ghost story, is it?" he said, sitting down beside the princess and hastily adjusting his eyeglass, as though he couldn't begin to speak without this instrument.
"Why no, my dear fellow," said the astonished storyteller, shrugging his shoulders.
"Because I hate ghost stories," said Prince Hippolyte in a tone that suggested he only understood the meaning of his own words after he had said them.

He spoke with such self-assurance that his listeners could never be quite sure whether what he said was very witty or very stupid. He was dressed in a dark green coat and knee breeches the color of what he himself called "startled nymph's thigh," with shoes and silk stockings.

The vicomte told his story very neatly. It was an anecdote making the rounds at the time, about how the Duc d'Enghien had secretly gone to Paris to visit Mademoiselle George; that at her house he had come upon Bonaparte, who also enjoyed the famous actress's favors; and that in the duc's presence, Napoleon happened to fall into one of the fainting spells he was prone to, leaving him entirely at the duc's mercy. The duc spared him — and this act of mercy Bonaparte later repaid with execution.
The story was very pretty and engaging, especially the part where the rivals suddenly recognized each other, and the ladies looked moved.
"Charming!" said Anna Pavlovna, glancing inquiringly at the little princess.
"Charming!" whispered the little princess, pushing her needle into her embroidery as if to prove that the story was so fascinating it prevented her from continuing her work.

The vicomte appreciated this silent praise and, smiling gratefully, prepared to go on. But just then Anna Pavlovna, who had been keeping a watchful eye on the young man who made her so nervous, noticed that Pierre was talking too loudly and too intensely with the abbé, and hurried over to intervene. Pierre had managed to start a conversation with the abbé about the balance of power, and the abbé, clearly drawn in by the young man's earnest enthusiasm, was laying out his favorite theory. Both were talking and listening with too much natural eagerness — which was exactly what Anna Pavlovna disapproved of.

"The means are the balance of power in Europe and the rights of the people," the abbé was saying. "All that's needed is for one powerful nation like Russia — however barbaric she may be called — to place herself unselfishly at the head of an alliance dedicated to maintaining the European balance of power, and the world would be saved!"
"But how do you actually achieve that balance?" Pierre began.

At that moment Anna Pavlovna appeared and, looking sternly at Pierre, asked the Italian how he was finding the Russian climate. The Italian's face changed instantly, taking on an offensively affected, sugary expression — clearly his habitual manner when speaking with women.

"I am so enchanted by the brilliance of the wit and culture in this society — especially the feminine society — in which I have had the honor of being received, that I have not yet had time to think about the climate," he said (in French).
Keeping both the abbé and Pierre from escaping, Anna Pavlovna brought them into the larger circle, the better to keep them under observation.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 4
paragraphs: Just then another guest entered the drawing room: Prince Andrew Bolkonski, the little princess's husband. He was a very handsome young man of medium height, with firm, sharply defined features. Everything about him — from his weary, bored expression to his quiet, measured stride — stood in the sharpest contrast to his lively little wife. It was clear that he not only knew everyone in the room but found them all so tiresome that it exhausted him to look at or listen to them. And of all the faces he found so tedious, none seemed to bore him quite as much as his pretty wife's. He turned away from her with a grimace that marred his handsome face, kissed Anna Pavlovna's hand, and squinting slightly, surveyed the entire company.
"You are off to the war, Prince?" said Anna Pavlovna.
"General Kutuzov" — said Bolkonski, speaking French and stressing the last syllable of the general's name in the French manner — "has been kind enough to take me on as an aide-de-camp..."
"And Lise, your wife?"
"She will go to the country."
"Aren't you ashamed to deprive us of your charming wife?"

"André," said his wife (in French), addressing her husband in the same flirtatious way she spoke to other men, "the vicomte has been telling us the most wonderful story about Mademoiselle George and Bonaparte!"

Prince Andrew screwed up his eyes and looked away. Pierre, who had been watching him with glad, affectionate eyes from the moment he entered the room, now came up and took his arm. Before Prince Andrew could even look around, he frowned again — annoyed at whoever was touching his arm — but when he saw Pierre's beaming face, he broke into an unexpectedly warm and genuine smile.
"Well, well! So you've made it into high society too?" he said to Pierre.
"I knew you would be here," replied Pierre. "I'll come to supper with you. May I?" he added in a low voice, so as not to disturb the vicomte, who was still telling his story.

"No, impossible!" said Prince Andrew, laughing and squeezing Pierre's hand to show that there was no need to ask. He wanted to say something more, but just then Prince Vasili and his daughter stood up to leave, and the two young men rose to let them pass.

"You must excuse me, dear Vicomte," said Prince Vasili to the Frenchman (in French), holding him by the sleeve in a friendly way to keep him from getting up. "This wretched party at the ambassador's is robbing me of a pleasure and forcing me to cut you short. I'm truly sorry to leave your delightful gathering," he said, turning to Anna Pavlovna.

His daughter, Princess Helene, passed between the chairs, lightly gathering up the folds of her gown, her smile shining even more brilliantly on her beautiful face. Pierre gazed at her with fascinated, almost frightened eyes as she swept past him.
"Very lovely," said Prince Andrew.
"Very," said Pierre.

As he passed, Prince Vasili seized Pierre's hand and said to Anna Pavlovna, "Educate this bear for me! He's been staying at my house for a whole month and this is the first time I've seen him out in society. Nothing is as essential for a young man as the company of intelligent women."

Anna Pavlovna smiled and promised to take Pierre in hand. She knew his father was connected to Prince Vasili. The elderly lady who had been sitting with the old aunt rose quickly and hurried after Prince Vasili into the entrance hall. All the artificial interest she had been showing dropped away from her kind, careworn face, which now expressed nothing but anxiety and fear.
"What about my son Boris, Prince?" she said, following him into the hall. "I can't stay in Petersburg any longer. Tell me — what news can I bring back to my poor boy?"

Although Prince Vasili listened reluctantly and rather rudely to the elderly lady, even showing signs of impatience, she gave him a fawning, pleading smile and seized his hand to prevent him from leaving.
"What would it cost you to put in a word with the Emperor? Then he would be transferred to the Guards immediately," she said.

"Believe me, Princess, I'm prepared to do everything I can," answered Prince Vasili, "but it's difficult for me to petition the Emperor. I'd advise you to go through Prince Golitsyn to Rumyantsev. That would be the best approach."

The elderly lady was Princess Drubetskaya, from one of the finest families in Russia, but she was poor and had been out of society for so long that she had lost all her old connections. She had come to Petersburg for the sole purpose of securing a position in the Guards for her only son. In fact, it was specifically to see Prince Vasili that she had obtained an invitation to Anna Pavlovna's reception and had sat through the vicomte's story. Prince Vasili's words alarmed her; a bitter expression clouded her once-handsome face — but only for a moment. Then she smiled again and gripped Prince Vasili's arm even more tightly.

"Listen to me, Prince," she said. "I have never asked you for anything, and I never will again. I have never reminded you of my father's friendship with you. But now I beg you, for God's sake, do this for my son — and I shall always consider you my benefactor," she added quickly. "No, don't be angry — just promise me! I've already asked Golitsyn and he refused. Be the kindhearted man you have always been," she said, trying to smile though tears stood in her eyes.
"Papa, we're going to be late," said Princess Helene (in French), turning her beautiful head and glancing back over her sculpted shoulder as she waited by the door.

Social influence, however, is a form of capital that must be spent carefully if it is to last. Prince Vasili understood this, and having realized that if he used his influence on behalf of everyone who came asking, he would soon have none left for himself, he had become cautious about spending it. But in Princess Drubetskaya's case, after her second appeal, he felt something close to a pang of conscience. She had reminded him of something that was perfectly true: he owed his first steps in his career to her father. Moreover, he could see from her manner that she was one of those women — mostly mothers — who, once they have set their minds on something, will not rest until they get what they want, and are fully prepared to keep insisting day after day, hour after hour, and if necessary, to make scenes. This last thought moved him.

"My dear Anna Mikhaylovna," he said (in French) with his usual familiar, weary tone, "it's nearly impossible for me to do what you're asking. But to prove my devotion to you and my respect for your father's memory, I will do the impossible. Your son will be transferred to the Guards. Here is my hand on it. Are you satisfied?"
"My dear benefactor! This is what I expected from you — I knew your kindness!" He turned to go.

"Wait — just one more thing! When he's been transferred to the Guards..." She hesitated. "You're on good terms with Mikhail Ilarionovich Kutuzov... recommend Boris to him as an adjutant! Then I'll be at peace, and then..."
Prince Vasili smiled.

"No, that I can't promise. You have no idea how Kutuzov is being hounded since his appointment as Commander-in-Chief. He told me himself that every lady in Moscow has conspired to foist her son on him as an adjutant."
"No, but do promise! I won't let you go! My dear benefactor..."
"Papa," said his beautiful daughter (in French) in the same tone as before, "we're going to be late."
"Well, goodbye then! Goodbye! You hear her?" (in French)
"So tomorrow you'll speak to the Emperor?"
"Yes, definitely. But about Kutuzov — that I don't promise."

"Do promise, do promise, Vasili!" cried Anna Mikhaylovna (in French) as he left, wearing the smile of a flirtatious girl — which had probably once come naturally to her but was now very poorly suited to her careworn face.

She seemed to have forgotten her age, and out of long habit was employing all her old feminine wiles. But the moment the prince was gone, her face resumed its former cold, artificial expression. She went back to the group where the vicomte was still holding forth, and once again pretended to listen while she waited for the right moment to leave. Her mission was accomplished.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 5
paragraphs: "And what do you make of this latest farce — the coronation in Milan?" asked Anna Pavlovna. "And the comedy of the people of Genoa and Lucca presenting their petitions to Monsieur Bonaparte, while Monsieur Bonaparte sits on a throne and graciously grants the wishes of nations? It's beyond belief! It's enough to make your head spin! It's as if the whole world has gone mad."
Prince Andrew looked Anna Pavlovna straight in the face with a sardonic smile.
"'God has given it to me — let anyone who touches it beware!'" he said (in French), then repeated the words in Italian: "'Dio mi l'ha dato. Guai a chi la tocchi!'"
* Dieu me la donne, gare à qui la touche!
"I hope this will be the last straw," Anna Pavlovna continued. "The sovereigns will not be able to tolerate this man who threatens everything."

"The sovereigns? I'm not speaking of Russia," said the vicomte (in French), politely but without hope. "The sovereigns, madame — what have they done for Louis XVII, for the Queen, for Madame Elizabeth? Nothing!" He grew more animated. "And believe me, they are reaping what they sowed when they betrayed the Bourbon cause. The sovereigns! They're sending ambassadors to congratulate the usurper."
He sighed disdainfully and shifted his position again.

Prince Hippolyte, who had been staring at the vicomte through his eyeglass for some time, suddenly turned his whole body toward the little princess and, asking her for a needle, began tracing the Condé coat of arms on the table. He explained it to her with as much gravity as if she had asked him to do it.
"A red baton, engrailed, on an azure field — the house of Condé," he said (in French).
The princess listened with a smile.

"If Bonaparte remains on the throne of France for another year," the vicomte continued, with the air of a man who, being better informed than anyone else on the subject, doesn't listen to others but follows his own train of thought, "things will have gone too far. Through intrigue, violence, exile, and executions, French society — I mean good French society — will have been destroyed forever, and then..."
He shrugged his shoulders and spread his hands. Pierre wanted to say something — the conversation interested him — but Anna Pavlovna, who had been watching him, cut in first.

"Emperor Alexander," she said, with the melancholy that always accompanied any mention she made of the imperial family, "has declared that he will leave it to the French people to choose their own form of government. And I believe that once they are free of the usurper, the entire nation will throw itself into the arms of its rightful king," she concluded, trying to be gracious toward the royalist émigré.
"That's doubtful," said Prince Andrew. "The vicomte is quite right in saying that things have already gone too far. I think it will be very difficult to go back to the old order."
"From what I've heard," said Pierre, blushing as he broke into the conversation, "almost the entire aristocracy has already gone over to Bonaparte's side."
"That's what the Bonapartists say," replied the vicomte, without looking at Pierre. "At the present time it's hard to know the true state of French public opinion."
"Bonaparte himself has said so," remarked Prince Andrew with a sarcastic smile.
It was clear that he didn't like the vicomte and was directing his remarks at him, even while avoiding his gaze.

"'I showed them the path to glory, but they did not follow it,'" Prince Andrew continued after a brief silence, again quoting Napoleon's words. "'I opened my antechambers and they came crowding in.' I don't know how far he was justified in saying that."

"Not in the least," replied the vicomte. "After the murder of the duc, even his most devoted admirers stopped calling him a hero. If to some people," he went on, turning to Anna Pavlovna, "he ever was a hero, after the murder of the duc there was one more martyr in heaven and one fewer hero on earth."

Before Anna Pavlovna and the others could smile their appreciation of this neat line, Pierre broke into the conversation again, and though Anna Pavlovna was certain he would say something inappropriate, she was unable to stop him.

"The execution of the Duc d'Enghien," declared Pierre, "was a political necessity, and it seems to me that Napoleon showed greatness of soul by taking the full responsibility for that act upon himself."
"God! My God!" murmured Anna Pavlovna (in French) in a horrified whisper.
"What, Monsieur Pierre — you think assassination shows greatness of soul?" said the little princess, smiling and pulling her embroidery closer.
"Oh! Oh!" exclaimed several voices.
"Capital!" said Prince Hippolyte in English, and began slapping his knee with his palm.
The vicomte merely shrugged his shoulders. Pierre looked solemnly at his audience over his spectacles and continued.

"I say this," he went on with growing intensity, "because the Bourbons fled from the Revolution and abandoned the people to chaos. Napoleon alone understood the Revolution and brought it under control, and so, for the general good, he could not stop short on account of one man's life."
"Won't you come over to the other table?" suggested Anna Pavlovna.
But Pierre went on without paying her any attention.

"No," he cried, growing more and more passionate, "Napoleon is great because he rose above the Revolution, stamped out its worst excesses, and preserved everything good in it — equality before the law, freedom of speech, freedom of the press — and that is the only reason he gained power."
"Yes — if, having gained power, he had restored it to the rightful king instead of using it to commit murder, then I would call him a great man," remarked the vicomte.

"He couldn't do that. The people gave him power so that he could rid them of the Bourbons, and because they recognized that he was a great man. The Revolution was a magnificent thing!" declared Pierre, betraying by this reckless and provocative statement his extreme youth and his eagerness to say everything that was on his mind.
"What? Revolution and regicide — a magnificent thing? Well, after that... But won't you come to the other table?" Anna Pavlovna repeated.
"Rousseau's Social Contract," said the vicomte (in French) with a condescending smile.
"I'm not talking about regicide. I'm talking about ideas."
"Yes — ideas of robbery, murder, and regicide," someone interjected in an ironic voice.
"Those were extremes, certainly, but they aren't the main point. What matters are the rights of man, the liberation from prejudice, equality before the law — and Napoleon has upheld all of these."

"Liberty and equality," said the vicomte with contempt, as though finally deciding to demonstrate to this young man how foolish his words were. "Grand phrases that have long been discredited. Who doesn't love liberty and equality? Even our Savior preached liberty and equality. Have people become happier since the Revolution? On the contrary. We wanted freedom, and Bonaparte has destroyed it."

Prince Andrew watched with an amused smile, looking from Pierre to the vicomte and from the vicomte to their hostess. In the first moment of Pierre's outburst, Anna Pavlovna had been horrified, despite all her social experience. But when she saw that Pierre's blasphemous words had not outraged the vicomte, and had satisfied herself that it was impossible to shut Pierre up, she rallied her forces and joined the vicomte in a vigorous counterattack on the young orator.
"But my dear Monsieur Pierre," she said (in French), "how do you explain the fact that a great man would execute a duke — or even an ordinary person — who is innocent and has not been tried?"
"I would like to ask," said the vicomte, "how monsieur explains the 18th Brumaire. Was that not a fraud? It was a swindle, pure and simple — nothing like the behavior of a great man!"
"And the prisoners he killed in Africa! That was horrible!" said the little princess, shrugging her shoulders.
"He's a despicable man, no matter what anyone says," remarked Prince Hippolyte.

Pierre, not knowing whom to answer, looked around at all of them and smiled. His smile was unlike the half-smiles of other people. When he smiled, his serious, even somewhat gloomy expression was instantly replaced by something else — a childlike, kind, even slightly foolish look that seemed to ask forgiveness.
The vicomte, who was meeting Pierre for the first time, saw clearly that this young radical was not nearly as dangerous as his words suggested. Everyone fell silent.

"How do you expect him to answer all of you at once?" said Prince Andrew. "Besides, when judging a statesman, you have to distinguish between his actions as a private individual, as a general, and as an emperor. At least that's how it seems to me."
"Yes, yes — exactly!" Pierre chimed in, delighted at this reinforcement.

"One must admit," Prince Andrew continued, "that Napoleon the man was great on the bridge at Arcola, and in the hospital at Jaffa where he clasped the hands of plague victims. But... there are other actions that are hard to justify."
Prince Andrew, who had clearly been trying to soften the awkwardness of Pierre's remarks, stood up and signaled to his wife that it was time to go.
Suddenly Prince Hippolyte jumped up, gestured for everyone's attention, and asked them all to sit down, then began:

"I was told the most charming Moscow story today, and I simply must share it with you. Excuse me, Vicomte — I have to tell it in Russian or the whole point will be lost." And Prince Hippolyte launched into his story in the kind of Russian a Frenchman would speak after about a year in Russia. Everyone waited, so insistently did he demand their attention.

"There is a lady in Moscow — une dame — and she is very stingy. She insists on having two footmen behind her carriage, and very big ones. That's what she likes. And she had a maid, also big. She said..."
Here Prince Hippolyte paused, visibly struggling to recall his thoughts.
"She said... Oh yes! She said, 'Girl' — to the maid — 'put on a livery, get up behind the carriage, and come with me while I make some calls.'"
Here Prince Hippolyte sputtered and burst out laughing long before his audience, which did not help the story. A few people, including the elderly lady and Anna Pavlovna, did manage a smile.

"She went. Suddenly there was a great gust of wind. The girl lost her hat and her long hair came tumbling down..." Here he could barely get the words out through his gasps of laughter: "And the whole world found out..."

And so the story ended. Although it was impossible to say why he had told it, or why it had to be told in Russian, still, Anna Pavlovna and the others appreciated Prince Hippolyte's social instinct in so neatly defusing Pierre's uncomfortable and graceless outburst. After the anecdote, the conversation dissolved into harmless small talk about the latest ball and the next one, about the theater, and about who would see whom, and when and where.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 6
paragraphs: After thanking Anna Pavlovna for her delightful evening, the guests began to leave.

Pierre was an awkward man. Heavyset, about average height, broad-shouldered, with enormous red hands, he had no idea — as people say — how to enter a drawing room and even less how to exit one gracefully. He was also hopelessly absent-minded. When he stood to go, he picked up the general's three-cornered hat instead of his own and stood there tugging at its plume until the general asked for it back. All of this clumsiness was redeemed, however, by his kind, simple, and genuinely modest expression. Anna Pavlovna turned to him with a Christian gentleness that conveyed forgiveness for his blunders, nodded, and said: "I hope to see you again, but I also hope you'll change your opinions, my dear Monsieur Pierre."

He made no reply and only bowed, but once again everyone noticed that smile of his — a smile that said nothing at all, except perhaps: "Opinions are opinions, but can't you see what a decent, good-natured fellow I am?" And everyone, including Anna Pavlovna, could feel this.

Prince Andrew had gone out into the hall and, with his shoulders turned to the footman helping him on with his cloak, listened with cold indifference to his wife chattering with Prince Hippolyte, who had also come out. Prince Hippolyte stood close to the pretty, pregnant princess, staring at her through his monocle.
"Go inside, Annette, or you'll catch cold," said the little princess (in French), taking leave of Anna Pavlovna. "It's settled," she added in a low voice.
Anna Pavlovna had already managed to speak with Lise about the match she was arranging between Anatole and the little princess's sister-in-law.
"I'm counting on you, my dear," said Anna Pavlovna, also speaking softly. "Write to her and let me know what her father thinks of it. Goodbye!" And she went back inside.
Prince Hippolyte walked up to the little princess and, leaning his face close to hers, began whispering something.

Two footmen — the princess's and his own — stood holding a shawl and a cloak, waiting for the conversation to end. They listened to the French being spoken, which meant nothing to them, with an expression that suggested they understood perfectly well but were too polite to show it. The princess, as always, spoke with a smile and listened with a laugh.
"I'm so glad I didn't go to the ambassador's," said Prince Hippolyte. "So dull. It's been a delightful evening, hasn't it? Delightful!"
"They say the ball will be wonderful," the princess replied, drawing up her soft little lip. "All the prettiest women in society will be there."

"Not all — because you won't be there. Not all," said Prince Hippolyte with a joyful smile. And snatching the shawl from the footman — even pushing the man aside — he began wrapping it around the princess. Whether from clumsiness or by design (no one could tell which), after adjusting the shawl he kept his arm around her for a long time, as though embracing her.
Still smiling, she moved gracefully away, turning to glance at her husband. Prince Andrew's eyes were closed — he looked utterly weary and sleepy.
"Ready?" he asked his wife, looking past her.

Prince Hippolyte hurriedly threw on his cloak, which in the latest fashion reached all the way to his heels, and stumbling in it, ran out to the porch after the princess, whom a footman was helping into the carriage.
"Princess, goodbye!" he cried (in French), stumbling over his words as much as his feet.
The princess, gathering up her skirt, was taking her seat in the dark carriage. Her husband was adjusting his saber. Prince Hippolyte, under the pretense of helping, was getting in everyone's way.
"Step aside, sir," said Prince Andrew in Russian, his tone cold and unpleasant, to Prince Hippolyte who was blocking his path.
"I'm expecting you, Pierre," said the same voice, but now gentle and affectionate.
The driver started and the carriage wheels clattered. Prince Hippolyte stood in the porch laughing convulsively as he waited for the vicomte, whom he had promised to take home.

"Well, my friend," said the vicomte (in French), settling himself beside Hippolyte in the carriage, "your little princess is very charming, very charming indeed — quite French." And he kissed his fingertips. Hippolyte burst out laughing.
"You know, for all your innocent airs you're quite the rascal," the vicomte continued. "I pity the poor husband — that little officer who puts on the airs of a king."
Hippolyte spluttered with laughter again. "And you were saying Russian ladies can't compare with the French? You just have to know how to handle them."

Pierre arrived at the house first and went into Prince Andrew's study as if he owned the place. Out of habit he immediately flopped down on the sofa, grabbed the first book his hand found on the shelf — it happened to be Caesar's Commentaries — and, propping himself on his elbow, began reading from the middle.
"What have you done to Mademoiselle Scherer? She's going to be quite ill after that," said Prince Andrew as he came into the study, rubbing his small white hands.
Pierre rolled his whole body over, making the sofa creak. He turned his eager face toward Prince Andrew, smiled, and waved his hand.
"That abbé is very interesting, but he's got it all wrong. In my opinion, perpetual peace is possible, but — how do I put it — not through a balance of political power..."
It was obvious that Prince Andrew had no interest in this kind of abstract discussion.
"You can't go around saying everything you think, my friend. Anyway, have you finally decided on anything? Are you going to be a guardsman or a diplomat?" asked Prince Andrew after a brief silence.
Pierre sat up on the sofa with his legs tucked under him.
"Honestly, I still don't know. I don't like either option."
"But you have to choose something! Your father expects it."

Pierre had been sent abroad at the age of ten with a tutor — an abbé — and had stayed away until he was twenty. When he returned to Moscow, his father dismissed the tutor and told the young man: "Now go to Petersburg, look around, and choose a career. I'll agree to anything. Here's a letter to Prince Vasili, and here's money. Write and tell me everything, and I'll help you however I can." Pierre had been trying to choose a career for three months now and had settled on nothing. It was this choice that Prince Andrew was asking about. Pierre rubbed his forehead.
"But he must be a Freemason," he said, referring to the abbé he had met that evening.
"That's all nonsense," Prince Andrew interrupted again. "Let's talk about something real. Have you been to the Horse Guards?"

"No, I haven't. But here's what I've been thinking, and I wanted to tell you: there's a war on against Napoleon. If it were a war for freedom, I'd understand it and I'd be the first to enlist. But to help England and Austria against the greatest man in the world — that's not right."

Prince Andrew merely shrugged at Pierre's naive words. He put on the look of a man who finds it pointless to reply to such nonsense, though in truth it would have been hard to give any better answer than the one he gave to this simplistic question.
"If nobody fought except from personal conviction, there would be no wars," he said.
"And that would be wonderful," said Pierre.
Prince Andrew smiled with irony.
"Very likely it would be wonderful, but it will never happen."
"Well then, why are you going to war?" asked Pierre.
"Why? I don't know. I have to. Besides, I'm going..." He paused. "I'm going because the life I'm leading here doesn't suit me!"

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 7
paragraphs: The rustle of a woman's dress was heard from the next room. Prince Andrew gave a start as if waking from sleep, and his face took on the expression it had worn in Anna Pavlovna's drawing room. Pierre swung his feet off the sofa. The princess came in. She had changed into a house dress that was just as fresh and elegant as the one before. Prince Andrew stood and politely pulled out a chair for her.

"How is it," she began, as usual in French, settling quickly and fussily into the armchair as she always did, "how is it that Annette never got married? How foolish you men all are for not marrying her! Forgive me for saying so, but you have no understanding of women whatsoever. What a debater you are, Monsieur Pierre!"

"And I'm still arguing with your husband. I can't understand why he wants to go to war," replied Pierre, speaking to the princess without any of the awkwardness young men usually show around young women.
The princess flinched. Pierre's words had clearly struck a nerve.

"That's exactly what I tell him!" she said. "I don't understand it at all — I simply cannot understand why men can't live without wars. How is it that we women want nothing of the kind, have no need for it? You be the judge between us. I'm always telling him: here he is, Uncle's aide-de-camp, the most brilliant position. Everyone knows him, everyone thinks so highly of him. Just the other day at the Apraksins' I heard a lady ask, 'Is that the famous Prince Andrew?' I really did!" She laughed. "He's received so well everywhere. He could easily become aide-de-camp to the Emperor himself. The Emperor spoke to him so graciously, you know. Annette and I were just discussing how to arrange it. What do you think?"
Pierre glanced at his friend and, seeing that he disliked the conversation, said nothing.
"When do you leave?" he asked.

"Oh, don't talk about his going — don't! I won't hear a word about it," said the princess in the same petulant, playful tone she had used with Hippolyte in the drawing room — a tone that was clearly out of place in this intimate family setting of which Pierre was practically a member. "Today, when I remembered that all these wonderful connections will have to be broken off... and then, you know, André..." She looked pointedly at her husband. "I'm frightened — I'm so frightened!" she whispered, and a shudder ran through her.
Her husband looked at her as though surprised to discover that someone besides Pierre and himself was in the room, and spoke to her with icy politeness.
"What exactly are you afraid of, Lise? I don't understand," he said.
"There — that's just like men! All of you — all egotists! Just on some whim of his own, God knows why, he abandons me and locks me away in the country all alone."
"With my father and sister, don't forget," said Prince Andrew gently.
"Alone all the same — without any of my friends. And he expects me not to be afraid."

Her voice had turned querulous now, and her lip was drawn up, giving her face not a joyful expression but an animal one — like a squirrel's. She paused, as if it would be improper to mention her pregnancy in front of Pierre, though that was the heart of the matter.
"I still can't understand what you're afraid of," said Prince Andrew slowly, his eyes fixed on his wife.
The princess blushed and threw up her arms in a gesture of despair.
"No, Andrew, I have to say it — you've changed. Oh, how you've changed..."
"Your doctor says you should go to bed earlier," said Prince Andrew. "You should go."
The princess said nothing, but suddenly her soft downy lip began to tremble. Prince Andrew stood up, shrugged his shoulders, and paced the room.
Pierre looked over his glasses with naive bewilderment — first at one, then at the other. He half rose as if to leave but then thought better of it.

"Why should I mind Monsieur Pierre being here?" the little princess exclaimed suddenly, her pretty face all at once crumpling into a tearful grimace. "I've wanted to ask you for so long, Andrew — why have you changed toward me? What have I done? You're going off to war and you have no pity for me. Why?"
"Lise!" was all Prince Andrew said. But that single word contained a plea, a warning, and above all the certainty that she herself would regret what she was saying. She rushed on regardless:
"You treat me like an invalid — or a child. I can see it perfectly well! Is this how you behaved six months ago?"
"Lise, I'm asking you to stop," said Prince Andrew, more firmly now.
Pierre, who had grown more and more distressed listening to all of this, stood up and went over to the princess. He seemed unable to bear the sight of tears and was on the verge of crying himself.

"Please calm yourself, Princess! It only seems that way because... I assure you, I've felt the same... because... No, forgive me! I'm an outsider — I have no business here. No, please don't upset yourself... Goodbye!"
Prince Andrew caught him by the hand.
"No, wait, Pierre! The princess is too kind to want to deprive me of the pleasure of spending the evening with you."
"No — he only thinks of himself," the princess muttered, unable to hold back her angry tears.
"Lise!" said Prince Andrew dryly, raising his voice to that pitch which signals that patience has run out.

Suddenly the angry, squirrel-like expression on the princess's pretty face transformed into a look of winning, pitiful fear. Her beautiful eyes darted sideways toward her husband's face, and her expression became timid and pleading — like a dog that rapidly but weakly wags its drooping tail.
"My God, my God!" she murmured (in French), and gathering up her skirt with one hand, she went to her husband and kissed him on the forehead.
"Good night, Lise," he said, rising and kissing her hand with the formal courtesy he might have shown a stranger.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 8
paragraphs: The two friends sat in silence. Neither wanted to be the first to speak. Pierre kept glancing at Prince Andrew; Prince Andrew rubbed his forehead with his small hand.
"Let's go have supper," he said with a sigh, moving toward the door.

They went into the elegant, newly decorated dining room, where everything was luxurious. From the table napkins to the silver, china, and glassware, everything bore that look of newness you find in the homes of the recently married. Halfway through supper, Prince Andrew leaned his elbows on the table with an expression of nervous agitation that Pierre had never seen on his face before, and began to speak — like a man who has been carrying something inside him for a long time and has suddenly decided to let it out.

"Never, never get married, my friend! That's my advice: don't marry until you can say to yourself that you've done everything you're capable of, and until you've stopped loving the woman you've chosen and can see her exactly as she is — or you'll make a terrible, irreversible mistake. Marry when you're old and good for nothing — otherwise everything that's good and noble in you will be lost. It'll all be wasted on trivialities. Yes! Yes! Yes! Don't look at me with such surprise. If you marry while you still expect something from yourself, you'll feel at every turn that for you it's all over, all finished — except for the drawing room, where you'll stand in a row alongside a court lackey and a fool! But what's the use of talking about it..." He waved his arm.
Pierre took off his glasses, which made his face look quite different, his good-natured expression even more apparent, and stared at his friend in astonishment.

"My wife," Prince Andrew went on, "is an excellent woman — one of those rare women around whom a man's honor is safe. But, my God, what wouldn't I give to be unmarried right now! You're the first and only person I've said this to, because I'm fond of you."

As he said this, Prince Andrew was nothing like the Bolkonski who had lounged in Anna Pavlovna's armchairs, murmuring French phrases through half-closed eyes. Every muscle of his thin face was quivering with agitation; his eyes, in which the spark of life had seemed completely extinguished, now blazed with a brilliant light. It was clear that the more lifeless he appeared in ordinary company, the more passionate he became in these moments of almost feverish intensity.

"You don't understand why I'm saying this," he continued, "but it's the whole story of a life. You talk about Bonaparte and his career" — though Pierre had not mentioned Bonaparte — "but when Bonaparte was working toward his goals, he moved forward step by step. He was free. He had nothing to think about except his aim, and he achieved it. But tie yourself to a woman and, like a prisoner in chains, you lose all freedom! And whatever hope and strength you have just weighs you down and fills you with regret. Drawing rooms, gossip, balls, vanity, triviality — that's the enchanted circle I can't break out of. I'm going to war now, the greatest war there has ever been, and I know nothing and I'm fit for nothing. I'm perfectly charming and I have a sharp wit," Prince Andrew continued, "and at Anna Pavlovna's everyone hangs on my words. And that mindless circle that my wife can't live without, and those women... If you only knew what society women are really like — what women in general are really like! My father is right. Selfish, vain, stupid, shallow in every way — that's what women are when you see them as they truly are! When you meet them in society, you think there's something there, but there's nothing — nothing — nothing! No, don't get married, my friend. Don't marry!" Prince Andrew concluded.
"It's strange to hear you say that," said Pierre. "You — you think you're incapable and your life is ruined? You have everything ahead of you, everything. And you..."
He didn't finish the sentence, but his tone made clear how highly he regarded his friend and how much he expected from his future.

"How can he talk like that?" Pierre wondered. He considered his friend a model of perfection because Prince Andrew possessed in the highest degree precisely those qualities Pierre himself lacked — qualities that could best be described as strength of will. Pierre was continually amazed by Prince Andrew's calm way of dealing with everyone, his extraordinary memory, his immense learning — he had read everything, knew everything, and had an opinion about everything — but above all by his capacity for work and study. And if Pierre was sometimes struck by Andrew's lack of talent for philosophical reflection — something Pierre was particularly drawn to — he saw even this not as a flaw but as a sign of strength.
Even in the best, most friendly, and simplest relationships, praise and encouragement are essential — just as grease is necessary to keep wheels turning smoothly.
"My part is played out," said Prince Andrew. "There's no point talking about me. Let's talk about you," he added after a pause, smiling at his own reassuring thoughts.
That smile was instantly reflected on Pierre's face.

"But what is there to say about me?" said Pierre, his expression relaxing into a carefree, cheerful grin. "What am I? An illegitimate son!" He suddenly turned bright red, and it was obvious this confession had cost him great effort. "No name and no fortune... And really..." But he didn't say what "really" was. "For now I'm free and doing all right. Only I haven't the faintest idea what to do with myself. I wanted to ask your advice seriously."
Prince Andrew looked at him warmly, yet even in that friendly, affectionate glance there was a consciousness of his own superiority.

"I'm fond of you, especially because you're the one truly alive person in our whole circle. Yes, you're doing fine! Choose whatever you want — it's all the same. You'll be fine anywhere. But listen: stop seeing the Kuragins and living that kind of life. It's so wrong for you — all that wild living, all that excess!"
"What can I say, my friend?" Pierre answered with a shrug. "Women, my friend — women!"
"I don't understand it," said Prince Andrew. "Women who are respectable — that's a different matter. But the Kuragin circle, 'women and wine' — I just don't understand it!"
Pierre was living at Prince Vasili Kuragin's house and sharing in the debauched lifestyle of his son Anatole — the very son they were planning to reform by marrying him off to Prince Andrew's sister.

"You know what?" said Pierre, as if suddenly struck by a brilliant idea. "Seriously, I've been thinking about this for a long time. Living the way I do, I can't make decisions properly — I can't think clearly about anything. My head aches and I spend all my money. He asked me to come tonight, but I'm not going."
"You give me your word of honor not to go?"
"On my honor!"

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 9
paragraphs: It was past one in the morning when Pierre left his friend's house. It was a cloudless northern summer night. Pierre hailed an open cab, intending to drive straight home. But the closer he got to his house, the more impossible it seemed to go to sleep on a night like this. It was bright enough to see far down the empty street, and it felt more like dawn or dusk than the middle of the night. On the way, Pierre remembered that Anatole Kuragin was expecting the usual crowd for cards that evening, after which there would typically be a drinking session, ending with the kind of amusements Pierre was particularly fond of.
"I should go to Kuragin's," he thought.

But he immediately remembered his promise to Prince Andrew not to go. Then, as happens with people of weak character, he wanted so desperately to enjoy those familiar pleasures one more time that he decided to go anyway. The thought immediately came to him that his promise to Prince Andrew didn't really count, because he had already promised Prince Anatole he would come before he gave Andrew his word. "Besides," he told himself, "all these 'words of honor' are just social conventions with no real meaning — especially when you consider that you could be dead by tomorrow, or something so extraordinary might happen that honor and dishonor become equally meaningless!" Pierre often talked himself out of his own decisions with reasoning like this. He went to Kuragin's.

When he reached the large house near the Horse Guards barracks where Anatole lived, Pierre walked through the lit entrance, climbed the stairs, and went in through the open door. There was no one in the front hall; empty bottles, cloaks, and boots were scattered around; there was a smell of alcohol, and from somewhere deeper in the house came shouting and the sound of voices.

Cards and supper were over, but the guests had not yet left. Pierre tossed off his cloak and entered the first room, where the remains of supper lay on the table. A footman, thinking no one was watching, was secretly finishing off what was left in the glasses. From a third room came bursts of laughter, the shouting of familiar voices, the growling of a bear, and general chaos. About eight or nine young men were crowded anxiously around an open window. Three others were roughhousing with a young bear — one pulling it by its chain, trying to set it on the others.
"A hundred on Stevens!" shouted one.
"No holding on!" cried another.
"I'm betting on Dolokhov!" yelled a third. "Kuragin, separate their hands!"
"Leave the bear alone — there's a bet to settle!"
"One go — or he loses!" shouted a fourth.

"Jacob, bring a bottle!" shouted the host — a tall, handsome young man standing in the middle of the group, coatless, his fine linen shirt unbuttoned at the chest. "Hold on, boys — here's Petya! Good man!" he called out, turning to Pierre.

From the window, another voice rang out — a man of medium height with clear blue eyes, his tone strikingly sober among all the drunken shouting: "Come here — settle the bets!" This was Dolokhov, an officer of the Semenov regiment, a notorious gambler and duelist who was living with Anatole. Pierre smiled and looked around cheerfully.
"I don't understand. What's going on?"
"Wait — he hasn't had enough to drink yet! A bottle here," said Anatole, and snatching a glass from the table, he went over to Pierre.
"First things first — you have to drink!"

Pierre drained one glass after another, peering from under his brows at the rowdy guests who had crowded back around the window, and listening to their chatter. Anatole kept refilling Pierre's glass while explaining that Dolokhov had made a bet with Stevens, an English naval officer, that he could drink an entire bottle of rum while sitting on the outer ledge of the third-floor window with his legs dangling over the edge.
"Come on, drink it all," said Anatole, handing Pierre the last glass, "or I won't let you go!"
"No, that's enough," said Pierre, pushing Anatole aside, and he walked up to the window.
Dolokhov was gripping the Englishman's hand and repeating the terms of the bet clearly and precisely, addressing himself mainly to Anatole and Pierre.

Dolokhov was of medium height, with curly hair and light blue eyes. He was about twenty-five. Like all infantry officers, he wore no mustache, so his mouth — the most striking feature of his face — was clearly visible. The lines of that mouth were remarkably well defined. The middle of his upper lip formed a sharp point and pressed firmly against the lower one, and something like two separate smiles played constantly around the corners; combined with the bold, insolent intelligence in his eyes, this created a face impossible to overlook. Dolokhov was a man without money or connections. Yet despite the fact that Anatole spent tens of thousands of rubles, Dolokhov lived with him and had established himself so firmly that everyone who knew them — including Anatole himself — respected Dolokhov more than they respected Anatole. He could play any card game and nearly always won. No matter how much he drank, he never lost his composure. Both Kuragin and Dolokhov were at that time notorious among the wild set of Petersburg.

The bottle of rum was brought. Two footmen, clearly rattled by the shouting and orders of the young gentlemen, were working to force out the window frame that prevented anyone from sitting on the outer sill.
Anatole strutted up to the window with his usual swagger. He wanted to smash something. Shoving the footmen aside, he grabbed the frame and tugged, but couldn't budge it. He smashed a pane of glass.
"You have a go, Hercules," he said, turning to Pierre.
Pierre grabbed the crossbeam, pulled hard, and ripped the oak frame out with a crash.
"Take it all the way out, or they'll think I'm holding on," said Dolokhov.
"Is the Englishman bragging? Hm? Are we ready?" said Anatole.
"All set," said Pierre, watching Dolokhov approach the window with the bottle of rum in his hand. Through the opening, the light of the sky was visible — dawn blending into the last glow of sunset.
Dolokhov jumped onto the windowsill, the bottle still in his hand. "Listen!" he called out, standing there and addressing the room. Everyone fell silent.

"I bet fifty imperials" — he spoke in French so the Englishman could understand, though his French wasn't very good — "I bet fifty imperials... or would you prefer to make it a hundred?" he added, turning to the Englishman.
"No, fifty," the Englishman replied.

"Fine. Fifty imperials that I will drink an entire bottle of rum without taking it from my mouth, sitting out there on that ledge" — he leaned down and pointed to the sloping surface outside the window — "without holding on to anything. Agreed?"
"Agreed," said the Englishman.
Anatole turned to the Englishman and, grasping one of his coat buttons and looking down at him — the Englishman was short — began repeating the terms of the wager in English.

"Wait!" Dolokhov shouted, banging the bottle on the windowsill to get everyone's attention. "Hold on, Kuragin. Listen! If anyone else does the same thing, I'll pay him a hundred imperials. Understood?"

The Englishman nodded but gave no sign of whether he intended to take up this challenge himself. Anatole wouldn't let go of him, and although the Englishman kept nodding to show he understood, Anatole went on translating Dolokhov's words into English. A thin young fellow — a hussar of the Life Guards who had been losing all evening — climbed onto the windowsill, leaned out, and looked down.
"Oh! Oh! Oh!" he murmured, staring down at the stone pavement.
"Get back!" Dolokhov shouted, shoving him away from the window. The young man stumbled awkwardly back into the room, tripping over his spurs.

Setting the bottle on the windowsill within easy reach, Dolokhov climbed slowly and carefully through the window and lowered his legs. He braced himself against both sides of the frame, settled into position, shifted a little to the right, then to the left, and picked up the bottle. Anatole brought two candles and set them on the sill, though it was already quite light. Dolokhov's back in its white shirt and his curly head were lit from both sides. Everyone crowded to the window — the Englishman in front. Pierre stood there smiling, saying nothing. One man, older than the rest, suddenly pushed forward with a look of alarm and anger and tried to grab Dolokhov's shirt.
"This is madness! He'll be killed!" said this more sensible man.
Anatole stopped him.
"Don't touch him! You'll startle him, and then he really will fall. Eh? What then? Eh?"
Dolokhov turned around and, gripping with both hands again, readjusted himself on his perch.
"If anyone interferes again," he said, squeezing the words out through his thin, compressed lips, "I'll throw him down there myself. Now then!"

With that, he turned back around, let go with his hands, took the bottle, and raised it to his lips. He threw his head back and lifted his free hand for balance. One of the footmen, who had bent down to pick up broken glass, froze in that position, his eyes locked on the window and on Dolokhov's back. Anatole stood rigid, eyes wide. The Englishman watched from the side, lips pursed. The man who had tried to stop it all ran to a corner and threw himself face-down on the sofa. Pierre covered his face with his hands — a faint smile lingering on his features even though his expression now showed nothing but horror and fear. Everyone was completely still. Pierre took his hands away from his eyes. Dolokhov was still sitting in the same position, only his head was thrown further back until his curly hair touched his shirt collar, and the hand holding the bottle rose higher and higher, trembling with the effort. The bottle was visibly emptying, rising higher still, his head tilting back even more. "Why is it taking so long?" thought Pierre. It felt like more than half an hour had passed. Suddenly Dolokhov's spine arched backward and his arm shook convulsively; this was enough to make his whole body start sliding on the sloped ledge. As he began to slip, his head and arm wavered even more with the strain. One hand moved as if to grab the windowsill, then pulled back without touching it. Pierre covered his eyes again and told himself he would never open them. Then suddenly he felt a commotion all around. He looked up: Dolokhov was standing on the windowsill, his face pale but radiant.
"It's empty."
He tossed the bottle to the Englishman, who caught it neatly. Dolokhov jumped back into the room. He reeked of rum.
"Bravo! Well done! Now that's a bet! Unbelievable!" came the shouts from all sides.
The Englishman pulled out his purse and began counting out the money. Dolokhov stood frowning, saying nothing. Pierre leapt up onto the windowsill.
"Who wants to bet me? I'll do the same thing!" he cried suddenly. "Forget the bet — just like that! Someone bring me a bottle! I'll do it! Bring a bottle!"
"Let him try, let him try," said Dolokhov with a smile.
"Are you insane? Absolutely not! No one's letting you do that! You get dizzy just on a staircase!" several voices cried at once.
"I'll drink it! Bring me a bottle of rum!" Pierre yelled, slamming the table with a drunken, determined fist and getting ready to climb out the window.
They grabbed him by the arms, but he was so strong that everyone who touched him went flying.
"No, you'll never manage him like that," said Anatole. "Wait — I'll talk him round. Listen! I'll take your bet tomorrow, but right now we're all going to ——'s."
"Let's go then!" cried Pierre. "Let's go! And we're bringing the bear!"
He grabbed the bear, lifted it in his arms, and began dancing around the room with it.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 10
